titles.593: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — thought vere≠falso and proprie≠figurate; Vir doctus equates both with personaliter
titles.594: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — did they sin vere or falso? False sin cannot be damned by a just judge
titles.595: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — proprie not figurate/metaphorice; penalty and sin answer each other
titles.596: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — born vere & proprie sinners; Augustine and great names deny damnation for another's sin alone
titles.597: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — Martyr vs Pighius; merit of true condemnation — 'by imputation'?

latin.593: PLAC. Putabam vere opponi falso, & proprie improprie sive infigurate, atque ita accipiebam; sed docet me nunc Vir doctus utrumque hoc loco idem valere quod personaliter, vel in propria persona.
latin.594: Quaero igitur, qui ita peccaverunt ut iustam & propriam condemnationem sint commeriti, verumne vere, an falso peccaverint? Falso, opinor, nemo dixerit. Qui enim dicitur ita peccasse ut iustam condemnationem sit promeritus, si potest probare id falso dici, fieri non potest ut ob eiusmodi peccatum damnetur ab iudice iusto.
latin.595: Rursus quaero an proprie dici possit peccasse, necne, hoc est, non figurate, aut metaphorice? Nemo etiam dixerit, peccasse tantum metaphorice aut figurate: cum enim poena & peccatum sibi mutuo respondeant, poena vere & proprie dicta supponit peccatum vere & proprie dictum, alienum quidem cum poena infligitur alicui ut vadi peccatoris, suum vero, cum infligitur ut peccatori poenam proprie dictam commerito.
latin.596: Nec negari potest quin nascamur ex Adamo vere & proprie peccatores, ab eoque peccatum vere & proprie sic dictum trahamus. Adde quod negat Augustinus, negant theologi alii magni nominis ob alienum peccatum quenquam damnari. Vide si placet verba Martyris a nobis laudata sup. pag. 196. ex loc. Com. Class. 2. cap. 1. §. 11. Necnon verba Calvini & Chamieci laudata sup. p. 95. 96. 97. 98.
latin.597: Addam haec pauca Martyris, ex eodem loco Com. §. 7. "Huic commento (intelligit commentum Pighii) nos nec possumus nec debemus acquiescere: nam ira Dei non nisi iuste provocatur. Neque enim ea eiusmodi est, ut temere aut fortuito inflammari possit. Quare oportet in natura nostra aliquid esse pravi, ad quod ulciscendum, ira divina excitetur." Alioqui, quomodo mereremur veram & proprie dictam condemnationem, si nullum esset nostrum eiusmodi condemnationis meritum? Est nostrum, inquies, imputatione. Facit ergo, inquam, imputatio ut mereamur poenam aeternam, quam alioqui non meremur.
latin.598: Id ne Dei aequitatem deceat, rogo te, Lector, diligenter considera. Cum enim scopus nobis propositus debeat esse Dei gloria, vide, quaeso, num id sit Deo gloriosum, & an eius aequitatem & iusticiam faciat clariorem. Vide etiam an deceat eius veritatem? peccavimus in Adamo, iustam mortis sententiam meriti sumus, idque sine dubio nec falso nec figurate: tamen non proprie sive personaliter peccavimus cum Adamus peccavit; sed tantum censemur apud Deum, ac si cum ipse peccavit, omnes peccassemus. Hoccine iudicium est secundum veritatem? gloriosum Deo?

pass_a.593: Placeus's first move: he had paired truly with falsely and properly with figurative/improper sense. Garrigues now collapses both adverbs into 'personally / in one's own person,' and Placeus marks that shift.
pass_a.594: He presses the dilemma under Garrigues's own equation: those who earned just condemnation—did they sin truly or falsely? No one will say falsely, because a just judge cannot damn for a falsely alleged sin.
pass_a.595: Second press on 'properly': not figure, not metaphor. Because penalty and sin must answer each other, a truly proper penalty already assumes a truly proper sin. He splits cases—another's sin when someone pays as surety for the sinner, and one's own when the penalty falls on the sinner as earned.
pass_a.596: He adds that we are born from Adam as truly proper sinners drawing a truly proper sin, then cites Augustine and other great names against damnation for another's sin alone, pointing readers to Martyr, Calvin, and Chamier already quoted in earlier pages.
pass_a.597: He brings Martyr against Pighius: divine wrath is kindled only justly, so something evil must already be in our nature. Then Placeus's own turn: how do we merit a truly proper condemnation if we have no such desert of our own? The reply 'it is ours by imputation' is flipped—imputation itself would then be what makes us merit an eternal penalty we otherwise do not merit.
pass_a.598: Tip for the reader: weigh whether that story fits God's equity, glory, and truth. Placeus restates the opponent's package—sinned in Adam and merited death neither falsely nor figuratively, yet not properly/personally, only reckoned as if all had sinned when Adam did—and asks whether such a judgment is according to the truth and glorious to God.

593: PLAC. I used to think "truly" was opposed to "falsely," and "properly" to "improperly" or "figuratively," and I took them that way; but the learned man now teaches me that in this place both mean the same as "personally," or "in one's own person."
594: I ask, then: those who have so sinned that they have earned a just and proper condemnation—have they sinned truly, or falsely? Falsely, I suppose, no one will say. For if someone is said to have so sinned that he has merited just condemnation, and yet one can prove that this is said falsely, it cannot be that he is damned by a just judge for a sin of that kind.
595: Again I ask whether he can be said to have sinned properly or not—that is, not figuratively or metaphorically. No one will say he sinned only metaphorically or figuratively: for since penalty and sin answer each other, a penalty truly and properly so called presupposes a sin truly and properly so called—another's, when the penalty is inflicted on someone as surety for the sinner; one's own, when it is inflicted on him as on a sinner who has earned a properly so-called penalty.
596: Nor can it be denied that we are born from Adam truly and properly sinners, and from him draw a sin truly and properly so called. Add that Augustine denies, and other theologians of great name deny, that anyone is damned for another's sin. See, if you will, the words of Martyr we cited above, p. 196, from Loci Communes, Class. 2, ch. 1, §11; and also Calvin's and Chamier's words cited above, pp. 95–98.
597: I will add these few words of Martyr from the same place, Loci §7: "We neither can nor ought to rest in this comment"—he means Pighius's comment—"for God's wrath is provoked only justly. Nor is it of such a kind that it can be kindled rashly or by chance. So there must be something evil in our nature, for the avenging of which the divine wrath is stirred." Otherwise, how would we merit a true and properly so-called condemnation, if we had no merit of that kind of condemnation of our own? "It is ours," you will say, "by imputation." So imputation, I reply, makes us merit an eternal penalty that otherwise we do not merit.
598: Whether that befits God's equity, I ask you, reader, to consider carefully. For since the end set before us ought to be God's glory, see, I pray, whether that is glorious to God, and whether it makes his equity and justice clearer. See also whether it befits his truth. We sinned in Adam; we merited the just sentence of death—and that without doubt neither falsely nor figuratively: yet we did not properly or personally sin when Adam sinned; we are only reckoned before God as if, when he himself sinned, we all had sinned. Is this judgment according to the truth? Glorious to God?
